title: OpenTelemetry Far and Wide
voice: Tyler Yahn's and Nikola Grcevski's authorized synthetic voices; not a recording of the presenters
status: Draft narration in authorized synthetic voices; actual demo timeout/fallback and waterfall captures. Monthly centralized-ownership cost scenario uses explicit hypothetical labor inputs.

chapters.title: OpenTelemetry Far and Wide

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Welcome everyone. I'm Tyler Yahn.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: And I'm Nikola Grcevski. Today we're following a slow customer checkout, from the first symptom to a fix.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: The application completes the request, but the customer is waiting. We'll follow that request across the system, add language detail, and change the code responsible. Then we'll use the OpenTelemetry Injector and a small demo operator to share that setup across the application.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: One customer problem, then a way for each of the teams in the organization to investigate theirs. Let's open the system.

chapters.purpose: Open a customer problem and promise a measured resolution, then make that investigation capability repeatable across the namespace.

chapters.title: One application, many places to look

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Here is our checkout application: eighteen services, with PostgreSQL and Redis. The Gateway hands the request to Checkout, which calls Inventory and four commerce branches. The map shows what can talk to what; the duration tells us the whole request is slow.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Every team can have a different definition of healthy. Following the request gives us one shared starting point.

chapters.purpose: Orient in the actual application without selecting a culprit.

chapters.title: Meet OBI

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: First, OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation, or OBI. It's a zero-code way to observe running Linux applications. It uses eBPF to watch application and network activity, then exports OpenTelemetry traces and metrics.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: We're getting a starting point across the application without asking each team to add a library or restart its service. That's a lot of visibility before the first instrumentation ticket. We showed this idea last year in Atlanta. Now OBI is version one and generally available.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: And this is more than a service map. OBI follows supported calls across service boundaries, including our HTTP, PostgreSQL, and Redis traffic. Let's deploy it on the nodes and let it discover the running applications.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: One deployment. Eighteen services to investigate. Much better odds than guessing which team to call. Let's open a request.

chapters.purpose: Introduce OBI before its acronym is used: eBPF observations of running Linux applications, zero app changes/restarts, traces and metrics. Show deployment only after explaining its value.

chapters.title: One request across the application

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Look what that one OBI deployment gave us. This is the slow request behind the opening number, followed across the application. Here are the HTTP calls and the PostgreSQL price query, before we've added a language agent to any service.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Different languages, one request we can follow. We've gone from a customer waiting for seconds to a specific set of service calls and durations. That's a huge head start for such a small setup. The customer is still waiting, though. Let's find the part we can change.

chapters.purpose: Give the connected-trace statement its own actual waterfall exemplar.

chapters.title: Follow the cart branch of this request

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Watch the plain topology turn into an observed request path. We can now ask which calls happened, which services handled them, and where the time went.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Here we're following the Cart branch through Catalog, Recommendations, and Promotions. This is one branch of the same request moving through the system.

chapters.purpose: Transform orientation into an observed path, using the captured request.

chapters.title: Find the failed connection on the request path

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Start with the waterfall. Gateway's long span includes its wait for Checkout, and Checkout's span includes its downstream work. The longest parent span doesn't tell us what to fix.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Look at this failed connection from Checkout instead. It consumes about two seconds before the successful product lookup and the other service calls.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Now we have somewhere specific to investigate: why is Checkout spending time on a connection that fails? OBI has exposed the failed attempt; language detail can connect it to the method and fallback in our code.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Let's open Checkout and follow that connection.

chapters.purpose: Select Checkout from the actual failed CONNECT span; use language detail to identify the calling method, timeout exception and working fallback.

chapters.title: Add Java zero-code instrumentation

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: We have source access here. Pricing runs before Inventory. We'll use the Java agent to time that method and expose the library calls inside it.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: This is OpenTelemetry's zero-code instrumentation. The agent supplies the instrumentation; we still need to make it available, add the startup setting, and configure where its data goes.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Here's the deployment change. The application image stays the same. We provide the agent, set the service identity and exporter, and enable the pricing-method span. Then we roll Checkout.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Zero code is useful, but hasn't made the release calendar disappear. Someone still needs the runtime knowledge, the settings, and a way to deploy the change.

chapters.purpose: Show actual source-informed configuration and the real direct-agent installation.

chapters.title: A failed attempt before a working fallback

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Here's a fresh request with the Java agent. Open PricingEngine.calculate. The long interval contains a failed HTTP connection, then a successful product-price lookup.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Open the failed HTTP span. Its error type is Java's SocketTimeoutException. The exception event says, Connect timed out. That is a connection timeout. The product-price lookup after it succeeds, so Checkout completes, but the customer pays for the failed attempt first.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: OBI got us to Checkout. The language agent exposed the failed attempt and the working fallback. Now we have a code change to investigate.

chapters.purpose: Show the actual HTTP span error.type and exception event before calling the failure a timeout; return to the successful price lookup.

chapters.title: Stop calling the retired backend

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: There it is. Pricing still calls a legacy backend that no longer exists. The connection times out after two seconds, then we read the price from the current product store. The fix is to use that store directly.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Instrumentation didn't fix the code. It enabled us to act. If we can collaborate with the owning team, we can bring a pull request instead of a vague report that their service is slow. Here is the customer impact, this is the trace showing the timeout, and now we have a change that removes it while keeping the price lookup.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: We're deploying that application change now. The Java agent and exporter settings stay the same.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: The rollout is ready. Let's send another customer request and look at its trace.

chapters.purpose: Show the actual Java source edit in Vim, retaining the working price lookup; offer a PR backed by the trace, then deploy the same fix.

chapters.title: The next checkout skips the failed call

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Here is the new request's waterfall. Expand Checkout and PricingEngine.calculate. The product-price query is still here. The failed legacy call is gone, and the rest of the request starts sooner.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Follow it through Inventory, the commerce branches, and the order write. We kept the useful work. The customer gets a faster checkout because we're no longer waiting for a backend that isn't there.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: This is the payoff: a customer symptom, an observed cause, a code change, and a fresh trace showing what changed.

chapters.purpose: Return directly to a real Grafana waterfall after deployment; show the missing failed attempt and retained successful backend path before aggregate metrics.

chapters.title: The improvement across repeated requests

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Across matched requests, the median checkout went from about two point two seconds to two hundred and twenty milliseconds. Pricing dropped from about two seconds to under four milliseconds. That supports the change we just followed in the waterfall: stop making the customer wait for a backend that is gone.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: That summary supports the trace we just saw. It is a local demo comparison, not a production benchmark. Next, how do we make the same diagnostic detail available to the other teams?

chapters.purpose: Summarize matched measured request durations only after the audience has seen the actual post-fix waterfall.

chapters.title: One fixed. Thirteen to equip.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: We've fixed this checkout. But getting to that answer needed runtime knowledge, configuration, access, and a deployment. How do the other teams get this detail without repeating all that setup?

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: In this demo, thirteen more services use runtimes supported by the OTel Injector. The Go services will keep their OBI coverage. Our next step is to share the setup across those thirteen.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: And share the routine work around it. Not every team has our access, our runtime knowledge, or an empty release queue.

chapters.purpose: Turn the resolved customer delay into the second tension: make the same diagnostic detail available to the other teams without repeating the direct setup.

chapters.title: From language opt-in to a shared namespace policy

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: To see what we're centralizing, here's the upstream Operator's opt-in configuration. Java and Python have different injection annotations, with an Instrumentation resource supplying their settings. You can put those annotations on workloads or a namespace.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: That already saves work. For this talk, we built RIO, the Runtime Instrumentation Operator, in OTelX. It's a demo operator that combines central namespace selection, the OpenTelemetry Injector, and managed rollouts. We want to bring this capability upstream, whether in the existing Operator or another form. That path still needs design and agreement.

chapters.purpose: Put upstream opt-in in context, then explain RIO as a talk-specific demonstration of functionality we want upstream; no agreed implementation or roadmap.

chapters.title: Install the namespace-driven controller

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Here we install the demo controller once. It builds on Jack Berg's prototype. The controller selects workloads and manages their rollout. The OpenTelemetry Injector handles supported runtimes and loads their agents.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: The payload, exporter, and exclusions are shared settings. Application owners don't each choose a language annotation and arrange a separate instrumentation rollout. Next comes the application choice: instrument this namespace.

chapters.purpose: Install the talk-specific controller and shared Injector settings once; demonstrate the workflow rather than recommend RIO as a production dependency.

chapters.title: Instrument this namespace

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Here is the selection rule: instrument demo-apps. We select the application boundary once. Unlike the language opt-in we just showed, this rule doesn't list languages or individual services.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Apply that rule, and the controller rolls the selected workloads. The Injector injects and supplies the OTel agents. Compatible services deployed into the namespace later inherit the same policy.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Now all the supported services are lit up. Checkout keeps its direct agent, thirteen more services gain language detail, and the four Go services keep OBI. The ongoing responsibility lives with the platform, instead of thirteen application teams repeating it. OBI is still running here. It detects services already exporting traces through an OpenTelemetry SDK and avoids duplicate tracing. We didn't have to reconfigure OBI for every service.

chapters.purpose: Show the actual single namespace selection and automatic rollout, then light the actual covered fleet using the captured result.

chapters.title: Open language detail in more services

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Back in the application view, we're looking at a new request through the instrumented fleet. We still have the system view, and now we can open language-level observations in more services.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Let's follow Catalog. These are the Java agent's database spans from that service. The same enrollment also covers the Node, Python, Ruby, and dot net services in this application.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: The namespace rule got us here without a separate instrumentation change from each application team. Checkout keeps its fix. Now the other teams have the language detail ready for their next investigation too.

chapters.purpose: Use the actual fleet trace, then inspect Catalog rather than returning only to Checkout.

chapters.title: The work around a deployment adds up

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Think about the direct setup we watched. We knew the runtime, had access, and controlled the release. How much happens before someone in a real organization can even begin?

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Find an owner. Explain the request. A ticket, a meeting, access, review, and a release slot. Then somebody switches away from their feature work.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: One namespace choice can remove repeated enrollment changes and keep shared settings consistent. The saving is more than typing fewer commands.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: It is fewer people arranging the same work. Count their active effort separately from the time spent waiting.

chapters.purpose: Connect the demonstrated workflow to people, coordination and waiting.

chapters.title: Reuse the workflow after day one

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: And setup is only the first bill. A new service arrives. An agent needs an update. A team needs to turn instrumentation off.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Compatible new services inherit the namespace choice. Updates reuse the shared rollout path. Configuration, documentation, and recovery instructions have one place to improve. A runtime change doesn't automatically mean a new onboarding project: OBI can keep the baseline for supported traffic, while language-level detail depends on the runtime.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: That can reduce drift and repeated troubleshooting. But the platform does not maintain itself.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Exactly. Compatibility, rollout, and recovery still need people. Their time goes into the calculation too.

chapters.purpose: Cover onboarding, updates, consistency, recovery, training and shared upkeep.

chapters.title: Make coverage the default

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: This is a sketch of adoption, not measured rollout data. Team-by-team ownership advances in steps: one service, then another. Busy teams create a long tail that may never reach full coverage.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: And the finish line moves. New services arrive. Someone rewrites a service from Java to Python, and the old instrumentation setup no longer fits. Coverage can drop while other teams are still catching up.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Central policy makes coverage the default. One rollout reaches the eligible services in scope, and new compatible workloads inherit it. The platform still tests and maintains that shared path.

chapters.purpose: Compare one central enrollment and inherited coverage with a team-by-team long tail; explain aloud that the paths are conceptual, not observed adoption data.

chapters.title: The cost of team-by-team ownership

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Let's keep the cost comparison in this demo. Eighteen services, thirteen of them still needing language instrumentation after our first example. These steps show setup and two years of monthly agent updates. Each jump is another release.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: With distributed ownership, each service owner arranges the work. With centralized control, we set up the namespace once and share each update. Both lines include upkeep; the centralized path still costs engineering time.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: Over two years, that frees two hundred and forty-seven engineering hours. At a hundred dollars an hour, that's twenty-four thousand seven hundred dollars. From setup and monthly updates, in the same small application we've been investigating.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: These are assumed person-hours valued at a hundred dollars an hour, not a measured cash saving. Include your own compatibility and support costs. We haven't priced the calendar time spent waiting for other teams.

chapters.purpose: Keep the cumulative setup/upkeep comparison in the same 18-service demo. Step up at each monthly release: 9.75 distributed hours versus 0.75 central hours. Over two years, show 266.5 versus 19.5 hours and emphasize 247 engineering hours freed, with their $24,700 assumed labor value secondary.

chapters.title: Less waiting. More services ready.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: We started with a customer waiting for checkout. OBI showed the failed connection. The Java agent connected it to pricing and its fallback. We removed the stale backend attempt, then returned to the actual request trace to see the change.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: Then one namespace choice carried language instrumentation across the supported services. The next team can start with useful detail instead of starting another setup project.

turns.speaker: Tyler
turns.text: The customer gets a faster checkout. The teams get a shared way to investigate the next slow request. That is what the traces and the automation were for.

turns.speaker: Nikola
turns.text: The demo shows the idea. We want an upstream home for this workflow, with the design still open. Find the wait. Fix the cause. Make the next investigation easier. Let's take your questions.

chapters.purpose: Close the customer-latency loop and the shared-workflow loop together; leave both outcomes visible during questions.
